result:
A race condition is a bug where the result depends on the timing of two or more processes touching the same resource, so it works most of the time and fails unpredictably. With a shared log, two scripts writing at once can interleave their output mid-line.

To avoid it, take an exclusive lock around the write with `flock`:

```sh
{
  flock 9
  echo "$(date -Is) something happened" >&9
} 9>>/var/log/shared.log
```

Each writer waits for the lock, appends, and releases it when the block closes fd 9. Every script that writes to the file must do the same.

A single short `echo ... >> file` is already safe on a local filesystem, because `>>` opens with `O_APPEND` and each small write lands whole. You need the lock when one entry spans several commands or lines, or when the output is large.

Left out: NFS, where `flock` can be unreliable; there, have a single process own the file (for example, send entries through `logger` to syslog).
